youtube.aciklama:
What is vestibular migraine, and how is it recognized? In this lesson we cover the Barany Society and International Headache Society criteria (at least 5 attacks lasting 5 minutes to 72 hours), migraine features, hearing and vestibular test findings, and how to tell it apart from Meniere's disease.

AIHEAR Audiology Academy makes short, clear lessons for audiology students and professionals.

Sources: Lempert et al., Vestibular migraine: Diagnostic criteria, Journal of Vestibular Research (2012) and its update (2022); Headache Classification Committee of the International Headache Society, ICHD-3 (2018); Neuhauser et al., Migrainous vertigo: prevalence and impact on quality of life, Neurology (2006); Formeister et al., The epidemiology of vestibular migraine: a population-based survey study, Otology & Neurotology (2018); Jacobson and Shepard, Balance Function Assessment and Management.

This video is for educational purposes and does not replace diagnosis or treatment.

sahneler.alt: A common cause of recurrent dizziness
cumleler: Hello, and welcome to the AIHEAR Audiology Academy.
In this lesson we will learn about vestibular migraine, one of the common causes of recurrent spontaneous attacks of dizziness.
We will cover the Barany Society criteria, hearing and vestibular test findings, and how it differs from Meniere's disease.
Vestibular migraine refers to recurrent vestibular attacks that occur as part of migraine disease.
The person usually has a known past or current history of migraine.
An important point: vestibular attacks do not always come with headache; some attacks may have no headache at all.
Vestibular symptoms may appear years after migraine attacks with headache first began.
It is clearly more common in women than in men and can begin at any age.
Its prevalence in the general population is estimated at about one to two point seven percent.
In dizziness and headache clinics, it is one of the most frequent diagnoses.
In vestibular migraine, attacks can take different forms; the criteria count them together.
Spontaneous vertigo is a sense of spinning or self-motion that starts without a clear trigger.
Positional vertigo starts when head position changes, so it can be confused with benign paroxysmal positional vertigo, or BPPV.
Visually induced vertigo appears in response to crowded, moving or patterned scenes.
Head motion-induced vertigo is a sense of spinning or swaying that lasts as long as the head is moving.
Head motion-induced dizziness with nausea also counts, but a feeling of unsteadiness alone is not a vestibular symptom in the criteria.
Many people have a clear history of motion sickness, such as car sickness, since childhood.
The mechanism of vestibular migraine is not fully known.
There are two-way connections between the vestibular nuclei in the brainstem and structures linked to pain and migraine.
Neural and chemical processes activated during migraine are thought to affect these vestibular pathways as well.
Findings suggesting inner ear involvement in some people have also been reported.
The migraine brain is generally more sensitive to sensory input such as light, sound and motion.
This sensitivity helps explain why visually and motion-triggered symptoms are common.

cumleler.yazi: The vestibular migraine criteria were published jointly in 2012 by the Barany Society and the International Headache Society.
cumleler.ses: The vestibular migraine criteria were published jointly in twenty twelve by the Barany Society and the International Headache Society.

cumleler.yazi: The criteria were updated in 2022; the main content was kept.
cumleler.ses: The criteria were updated in twenty twenty two; the main content was kept.

cumleler: Definite vestibular migraine first requires at least five vestibular attacks.
The attacks must be moderate or severe; that is, they must limit or prevent the person's daily activities.
Each attack lasts between five minutes and seventy two hours.

cumleler.yazi: The person must have a history of migraine with or without aura under the International Classification of Headache Disorders, or ICHD.
cumleler.ses: The person must have a history of migraine with or without aura under the International Classification of Headache Disorders, or I C H D.

cumleler: At least half of the vestibular attacks must be accompanied by one or more migraine features.
Finally, the condition must not be better explained by another vestibular disorder or another headache diagnosis.

cumleler.yazi: These criteria also appear in the appendix of ICHD-3.
cumleler.ses: These criteria also appear in the appendix of I C H D three.

cumleler: The first migraine feature is a headache with particular characteristics.
This headache must have at least two of four characteristics.
They are: one-sided location, pulsating quality, moderate or severe intensity, and worsening with routine physical activity.
The second feature is sensitivity to light, photophobia, together with sensitivity to sound, phonophobia.
The third feature is visual aura, for example shimmering zigzag lines in the visual field.
The attack criterion may be met, but only one of the two, the migraine history or migraine features during attacks, may be present.
In that case, the term probable vestibular migraine is used.
Probable vestibular migraine may become a definite diagnosis during follow-up, or another diagnosis may emerge.
Separate criteria have been defined for children; we will cover them in the lesson on dizziness in children.
In vestibular migraine, vestibular tests done between attacks are often normal.
Some people show variable findings such as mild positional nystagmus, mildly impaired smooth pursuit, or a mild caloric asymmetry.

cumleler.yazi: Results of vHIT, the video head impulse test, are usually normal.
cumleler.ses: Results of V HIT, the video head impulse test, are usually normal.

cumleler: Nystagmus seen during an attack can be peripheral, central or mixed, which makes diagnosis harder.
Studies report ear symptoms such as tinnitus, ear fullness or reduced hearing in up to a third of people.
The audiogram may show a mild or fluctuating change.
But a documented, marked sensorineural loss that progresses over time, as in Meniere's disease, is not expected.
The condition most often confused with vestibular migraine is Meniere's disease; both can have recurrent attacks and ear symptoms.
Attack duration is an important clue; Meniere's attacks last twenty minutes to twelve hours.
Vestibular migraine attacks last between five minutes and seventy two hours, a much wider range.
In Meniere's disease, sensorineural loss that starts in the low frequencies and is documented on an audiogram is part of the criteria.
In Meniere's disease the loss progresses over the years; in vestibular migraine, marked progressive loss is not expected.
Migraine features can also occur in Meniere's attacks; on their own, they do not distinguish the two.
Caloric weakness is common in Meniere's disease, while the caloric test is usually normal in vestibular migraine.
The two diseases can also coexist in the same person; then the diagnosis becomes clear with follow-up and serial audiograms.
The factors that trigger vestibular migraine attacks are largely the same as those that trigger migraine attacks.
Irregular sleep, meaning too little sleep or more sleep than usual, is a common trigger.
Stress, and sometimes the end of a stressful period, can set off attacks.
In women, hormonal changes such as the menstrual period may be linked to attacks.
Bright or flickering light, noise and crowded places can also be triggers.
Some people describe a link between certain foods and attacks; this link varies from person to person.
Keeping an attack diary helps the person recognize their own triggers.
The audiologist asks in detail about the duration, frequency and triggers of attacks and about migraine features.
When needed, the audiogram is repeated during and between attacks and assessed with Meniere's disease in mind.
The vestibular test battery helps look for other causes, such as unilateral loss or BPPV.
Diagnosis and treatment are the physician's decisions; treatment includes managing triggers and migraine therapies the physician sees fit.
There are studies showing that vestibular rehabilitation helps imbalance and motion sensitivity that persist between attacks.

sahneler.metin: In recurrent dizziness, always ask about migraine history and light or sound sensitivity during attacks; patients may not mention them on their own.
cumleler: A tip from the field: when patients come in for dizziness, they often do not mention headache.
Ask specifically about migraine history, migraine in the family, and discomfort from light or sound during attacks.
A history of motion sickness, such as car sickness, is also a valuable clue for vestibular migraine.
Having the patient record attack duration in minutes and hours makes it easier to separate it from Meniere's disease and BPPV.
Vestibular migraine is recurrent vestibular attacks in people with a migraine history; not every attack has headache.
A definite diagnosis requires at least five moderate or severe attacks lasting five minutes to seventy two hours.
At least half of the attacks have migraine features such as headache, light and sound sensitivity, or visual aura.
Tests are often normal; unlike Meniere's disease, documented and progressive sensorineural loss is not expected.

sahneler.soru: Attack duration range in vestibular migraine?
sahneler.aciklama: The Barany and ICHD criteria look for attacks lasting _5 minutes to 72 hours_.

cumleler.yazi: Test yourself: under the Barany criteria, what is the range of attack duration in vestibular migraine?

cumleler: The correct answer is B: five minutes to seventy two hours.
Twenty minutes to twelve hours is typical of Meniere's disease, and attacks shorter than a minute are typical of BPPV.
